simple: a short written description of a large program: what its parts are, how big they are, where it starts, what everything depends on, and how one request flows through it.
analogy: the floor plan you sketch on your first walk through an old house.
precise: in this course, a document of one to three pages, tied to one exact version of the code, that records (1) size and areas with numbers, (2) entry points, (3) hub modules, (4) the outline of the files on the path you care about and (5) at least one path traced end to end, where every step names the real file and line, directory or document section; curriculum milestone G1 asks for such "a written architecture map" with that naming rule in its acceptance test.
source: F12-20, this course's working definition, illustrated by its runs R1–R5 (pending verification)

simple: a place where the program starts running when someone uses it.
analogy: a door into the house.
precise: a function or file that the outside world calls first: a main function, a script that can be run directly, a system call handler, a request handler a framework calls, a callback a scheduler starts. Not the same as the ELF entry point of SP301 (the address where a loaded program starts), although a program's ELF entry point is one of its entry points in this wider sense. In the Python library mapped here, files that can be run directly contain a __main__ guard or are named __main__.py.
source: F12-20, this course's working definition, illustrated by its runs R1–R5 (pending verification)

simple: a part of the program that very many other parts use.
analogy: the main pipe every room is connected to.
precise: a module with high fan-in, the number of other files that import or include it; measured here by counting, for each top-level module name, the files containing an import or from line naming it. A change to a hub affects many callers; a hub is also a good place to start reading, because its interface is the vocabulary of the whole codebase.
source: F12-20, this course's working definition, illustrated by its runs R1–R5 (pending verification)

simple: the fixed text of a message with holes in it, filled in when the message is printed.
analogy: the shape of a stamp; the ink colour changes, the shape does not.
precise: a string such as "code %d, message %s" whose conversion specifications are replaced by values at run time; the printed log line is the format string with the holes filled, often after several functions have each added their own part. Python's % operator on strings works this way, and the server mapped here uses it to build its log lines.
source: F12-20, this course's working definition, illustrated by its runs R1–R5 (pending verification)

simple: a few lines you add, temporarily, to a program so that it tells you what it is doing at one point.
analogy: opening one small inspection hatch in a wall instead of knocking the wall down.
precise: code inserted without changing the program's behaviour (here, a subclass that overrides one method, prints where it was called from, and calls the original) to turn a question about the running program into an observation; Listing 2 is one. Not the same as a driver's probe function in DR301 or a hardware debug probe in HW303.
source: F12-20, this course's working definition, illustrated by its runs R1–R5 (pending verification)

simple: what you learn by reading the code versus what you learn by running it.
analogy: reading the floor plan versus turning on the tap and watching where the water goes.
precise: static evidence comes from the source without executing it (search results, outlines, import counts); dynamic evidence comes from an execution (logs, traces, a probe's output, a stack sample). Static evidence shows what can happen; dynamic evidence shows what did happen in one run. A map uses both and says which is which.
source: F12-20, this course's working definition, illustrated by its runs R1–R5 (pending verification)

simple: the program builds the name of the function to call from data, while it runs, so no line of the source calls that function by its name.
analogy: a doorbell panel where the visitor types the flat number; no wire runs from the street to one particular flat.
precise: a call through a run-time lookup (in Python, getattr(self, 'do_' + self.command) in the request handler mapped here; in C, a table of function pointers; in C++, a virtual call or a registry keyed by a string). Text search for callers of such a function finds none.
source: F12-20, this course's working definition, illustrated by its runs R1–R5 (pending verification)

simple: the list of every place one request passes through, from where it starts to where it is answered.
analogy: the pipe from the shower back to the street, with every joint written down.
precise: the ordered sequence of hops (functions, modules, processes, devices) that handle one request, each recorded with its location in a named version of the code or document and with the evidence that the request passed there; the answer usually travels back by a different route (a return, an interrupt, a callback), which is part of the path. This course writes request paths in the format of curriculum milestone G1.
source: F12-21, this course's working definition; Linux, QEMU, PX4 and ROS 2 names recalled, pending verification against D1–D6 of F12-21

simple: one step of a request path where something about the request changes.
analogy: a joint where the pipe changes size, material or owner.
precise: a point on a request path where ownership, representation, size or timing of the request changes: a library call becomes a system call, a file offset becomes a disk block, a request waits in a queue, a message is copied into another process. Hops are where requests are buffered, split, merged, delayed or dropped, and therefore where bugs and latency hide.
source: F12-21, this course's working definition; Linux, QEMU, PX4 and ROS 2 names recalled, pending verification against D1–D6 of F12-21

simple: a snapshot of which kernel functions a thread is inside at one moment, from the innermost outwards.
analogy: a photograph of the pipe joints the water is passing through right now.
precise: the list of return addresses on a task's kernel stack, resolved to function names, as Linux prints it in /proc/<pid>/task/<tid>/stack (readable by root in the F12-21 build); many samples of a busy thread show its kernel call chains and how often each occurs. A sample is statistical evidence: a hop that is fast is seen rarely.
source: F12-21, this course's working definition; Linux, QEMU, PX4 and ROS 2 names recalled, pending verification against D1–D6 of F12-21

simple: asking the operating system to read from the disk itself every time, without keeping a copy in memory.
analogy: drawing water straight from the main instead of from the attic tank.
precise: a flag to open() on Linux that asks for transfers between the user buffer and the device without the page cache, with alignment requirements on buffer, offset and length that the open(2) manual page describes ; used in Listing 2 so that every read() reaches the block layer.
source: F12-21, this course's working definition; Linux, QEMU, PX4 and ROS 2 names recalled, pending verification against D1–D6 of F12-21

simple: the part of the kernel that collects disk requests from file systems and hands them to disk drivers.
analogy: the manifold where pipes from many rooms join before the main.
precise: the Linux subsystem between file systems and block device drivers; its multi-queue design (blk-mq) keeps software and hardware queues and calls the driver's queue function to dispatch each request ; in this build's kernel the observed chain enters it at blk_finish_plug and leaves it at the driver's virtio_queue_rq.
source: F12-21, this course's working definition; Linux, QEMU, PX4 and ROS 2 names recalled, pending verification against D1–D6 of F12-21

simple: a message an emulator prints each time something chosen happens inside the emulated hardware.
analogy: a water meter at the street that writes down every litre that passes.
precise: a named probe point in QEMU's device models, enabled with -trace <name>, that prints the event's fields when it fires; this build used pci_nvme_admin_cmd, pci_nvme_io_cmd and pci_nvme_read of QEMU 8.2.2's NVMe controller.
source: F12-21, this course's working definition; Linux, QEMU, PX4 and ROS 2 names recalled, pending verification against D1–D6 of F12-21

simple: how old the measurement inside a message is when someone uses it.
analogy: how long the water has been in the pipes when it comes out of the shower.
precise: the time between the sample's measurement and its use at a given hop; the sum of the latencies the hops before it added. A periodic hop (one that runs on a timer and reads the newest message) adds between zero and one period, depending on phase, and can skip messages.
source: F12-21, this course's working definition; Linux, QEMU, PX4 and ROS 2 names recalled, pending verification against D1–D6 of F12-21

simple: code that people depend on but nobody fully understands, and that has no tests to tell you when you break it.
analogy: an old house a family still lives in.
precise: in this course, code that is in use (other code, tools or people depend on its behaviour) and whose behaviour is not pinned down by tests or a specification, so that a change cannot be checked against anything; age is not the criterion. D1 is the course card's reference for working with such code ; the definition here is this course's working definition, to be compared with D1's at the fact-check.
source: F12-22, this course's working definition; technique names recalled from Feathers, D1 of F12-22 (pending verification)

simple: a test that writes down what the code does today, right or wrong, so you notice when that changes.
analogy: photographing and testing every room, switch and tap before you touch anything.
precise: a test whose expected values are taken from running the existing code, not from a specification; it asserts "unchanged", not "correct". Listing 4 is one: it records twelve inputs and outputs of the legacy formatter.
source: F12-22, this course's working definition; technique names recalled from Feathers, D1 of F12-22 (pending verification)

simple: the saved output of a characterization test that later versions are compared with.
analogy: the photo album from the first day.
precise: a recorded set of outputs for a fixed, ordered set of inputs and controlled conditions (here: the same calls in the same order and a fixed clock), compared line by line against a new version; a difference is a behaviour change to be explained. Listing 6 compares the refactored formatter with it; the forensic lab compares a cleanup with it.
source: F12-22, this course's working definition; technique names recalled from Feathers, D1 of F12-22 (pending verification)

simple: a place where you can change what the code uses, without changing the code itself at that place.
analogy: a junction box where one cable can be disconnected to test a room alone.
precise: a point in a program where a dependency can be replaced from outside: a function pointer or virtual function (an object seam), a different definition chosen at link time (a link seam), a macro (a preprocessor seam). Listing 3's diff creates one: the clock is read through a function pointer that a test can point to a fixed clock. The names of the seam kinds are recalled from D1 (see the unverified box in Layer 2).
source: F12-22, this course's working definition; technique names recalled from Feathers, D1 of F12-22 (pending verification)

simple: something that changes what a function returns, but is not one of its arguments.
analogy: the porch light that depends on the hall switch, which nobody mentions.
precise: any state a function reads besides its parameters: a global or static variable, the clock, the environment, a file, a device register, the order of earlier calls. Hidden inputs make the same call return different results and must be controlled before behaviour can be recorded.
source: F12-22, this course's working definition; technique names recalled from Feathers, D1 of F12-22 (pending verification)

simple: writing a new feature as new code next to the old code, with its own tests, and calling it from one place.
analogy: a new room built beside the old one and joined at one door.
precise: a change technique in which new behaviour is implemented in a new function or class, developed with tests, and invoked from the legacy code at a single point, so that the untested code changes by as little as possible; cellVolts in Listing 5 is sprouted, and its call is guarded so that the old behaviour is unchanged when the feature is not used. The name is recalled from D1.
source: F12-22, this course's working definition; technique names recalled from Feathers, D1 of F12-22 (pending verification)

simple: changing how the code is written without changing anything it does.
analogy: rewiring a room so that every switch still does exactly what it did.
precise: a change of structure after which every observable output is identical for every recorded input; checked here by comparing with the golden master (12 of 12 identical in the F12-22 lab). A change that alters any recorded output is not a refactoring, whatever its commit message says.
source: F12-22, this course's working definition; technique names recalled from Feathers, D1 of F12-22 (pending verification)
